_comment: CANONICAL glossary. Mirrored by web/src/lib/glossary.ts; parity enforced by web/src/lib/glossary.parity.test.ts. Edit both together.

lane.definition: A shipping route between two specific places that goods can travel along.
lane.example: Supplier SUP-001 to factory PLANT-001 is one lane.

echelon.definition: One level of the supply chain, such as all the factories or all the warehouses.
echelon.example: This network has four: suppliers, factories, distribution centers, and customers.

bom.definition: The recipe for a product: which parts go into it, and how many of each.
bom.example: One finished product might need 3 of one subassembly and 1 of another.

lead_time.definition: How long you wait between placing an order and actually receiving it.
lead_time.example: A 9-day lead time means today's order arrives in 9 days.

fill_rate.definition: The share of what customers asked for that you were able to give them on time.
fill_rate.example: 96% fill rate means 96 of every 100 units ordered shipped when promised.

days_of_inventory.definition: How many days you could keep selling before running out, at the current rate.
days_of_inventory.example: 18 days of inventory means stock runs out in 18 days if nothing is replenished.

s_S_policy.definition: A restocking rule: when stock drops to the lower number, order enough to bring it back up to the higher one.
s_S_policy.example: With s=20 and S=100, hitting 20 units triggers an order of 80.

safety_stock.definition: Extra stock held on purpose, as a cushion against demand or delivery surprises.

backorder.definition: An order you could not fill right away but the customer is still waiting for.

lost_sale.definition: An order you could not fill, and the customer gave up and went elsewhere.
lost_sale.example: The difference from a backorder is whether you keep the sale.

holding_cost.definition: What it costs to keep one unit sitting in storage for one period.

ordering_cost.definition: The fixed cost of placing one order, no matter how large that order is.

intermittent_demand.definition: Demand that stops and starts, with many periods of no orders at all.
intermittent_demand.example: Spare parts often behave this way; steady weekly orders do not.

auto_ets.definition: A forecasting method for demand that arrives steadily, which picks up trends and seasonal patterns.

croston_sba.definition: A forecasting method built for demand that arrives in occasional bursts with gaps in between.

seed.definition: The starting number used to generate this data; the same seed always rebuilds exactly the same dataset.

period.definition: One step of time in the plan.
period.example: In this dataset a period is one week.

capacity.definition: The most that can be made, stored, or shipped in a single period.

service_target.definition: The service level promised to a customer, such as filling 96% of orders on time.

objective.definition: The single score the optimizer tries to make as small as possible, combining every cost and penalty.

criticality_tier.definition: How important it is that a given customer and product never runs short.
criticality_tier.example: This dataset labels the shock scenario's customers shock-critical.

on_hand.definition: Stock physically sitting at a location right now, available to use.

in_transit.definition: Stock that has already been shipped but has not arrived yet.

subassembly.definition: A part that is itself built from smaller parts before going into the final product.

days_of_cover.definition: How many days the stock on hand would last at the current rate of demand.
